That is quite correct, and I am quoting from this submission to show that the executive of the trades and labour congress did not consider that action by the provinces was the last word in the matter. Let me give a line or two more from the same submission:
It is a fact that the workers are not interfered with by the law in their desire to

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
organize, but experience has shown that that is not enough.
We say that, because experience has shown that there is interference with the workers in their endeavours to organize, and because the provinces so far have not passed legislation to prevent such interference, this bill has become necessary. That is why it has been introduced.
With further reference to legal rights, I believe it was Anatole France who said that the majestic equality of the law recognized that it was illegal for the rich as well as for the poor to sleep under bridges, but he also noted that the rich were not very often prosecuted for sleeping under bridges. The majestic equality of the law in this instance allows the workers to organize; but if the employer says they must not, they are in a very difficult position, and we say that the law should be amended so as to guarantee that right to them. The law says that the employees as well as the employer have the right to organize; but if the employer objects it becomes very difficult for the worker to exercise his legal right. It becomes almost impossible, without great sacrifice on the part of someone. Someone must sacrifice his job; on many occasions someone must sacrifice his hope of improving his future position, must sacrifice the future of his family.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house a case which I think I drew to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) last year, a case in which the Department of Labour tried to get a settlement. Burns & Company, Limited, in Vancouver had a dispute with its employees. Late in 1936 the workers of this comp:.~y formed a trade union. This was discovered by the company, and nineteen employees were dismissed, including the ten who were the executive of the union. After many attempts had been made by the provincial Department of Labour and the federal Department of Labour to effect a settlement, the provincial department appointed Mr. Justice J. C. McIntosh of Victoria as commissioner to investigate. The commissioner held sittings extending, I think, over ten or fifteen days, at which numerous witnesses were heard. I Should like to read briefly from his report, which states the conditions he found and the recommendations he made. This report is to be found in the June, 1937, issue of the Labour Gazette. He said:
The situation disclosed is unusual in labour disputes in Canada. No question of wage scale, hours of work or working conditions has arisen or is involved, as all such conditions were and are satisfactory to those affected, but consisted wholly of the activities of the newly formed labour union to which the majority of the employees belonged and the retaliatory reaction of the employing company's manager in relation thereto.
This union was formed with the sole purpose of advancing and protecting the interests of the company's employees and to improve the conditions of the workers, and with no ulterior motive.
No complaint was made by the manager of the services rendered by the employees, and an increase in pay was promised and later put into effect. He also informed the employees that they should seek to deal with the company in matters of mutual concern only through the medium of a plant or company union with no outside affiliations, this being the method adopted by most packing plants of consequence in Canada and the United States, of bargaining between the employees and employer, functioning in many cases side by side with a local union in such plants.
When the nineteen employees referred to were dismissed, a strike was called, and in referring to those dismissals the commissioner made this statement:
The intermingling of those nine employees against whom cause could be assigned, and those ten against whom no cause could be assigned except their activities as executives of their union, left only one implication. The manager must have known and anticipated that his action would culminate in a walkout of the employees, being members of the union.
As the commissioner could not get the parties concerned to agree, he proposed a plan of settlement himself. The report continues:
It is submitted as a reasonable plan for the reinstating in employment of the 131 employees affected-
Fot after the employees went on strike all of them were dismissed.
-apart from the nine mentioned, that the company shall reemploy fifty of those former employees in April, 1937, forty-one in May, 1937, and the remainder, being forty, in June, 1937, accelerating the numbers if the opportunity offers, at the scale of wages and working conditions now existing with the following provisoes:
Then he offers some suggestions for more harmonious working relations in future:
(a)	The selection of such employees shall be by some arrangement agreeable to the parties, married men in any event to be first selected when possible.
(b)	Upon this settlement being made effective the union shall immediately return the products of the company to the fair list.
(c)	There shall be no discrimination on the part of the company towards returning employees because of their former union activities.
(d)	The employees shall have the right to belong to any organization or association of their own choosing, and the company shall

recognize a committee elected by all of its employees to represent them in their dealings with the company's management.
(e)	The nine employees objected to by the company for cause shall have the privilege of appearing before the management of the company and being heard.
What I wish to bring particularly to the attention of the house is that despite the recommendations of the commissioner, very few of these employees have yet been taken back.
There is another point in this report which I think is very important. The commissioner stated that most, if not all, of the trouble developed because, first, the management did not understand trade union organization, and, second, the men themselves were not accustomed to trade union organization and their business agent did not approach his duties in the way that a more experienced trade union official would have done. And he made this recommendation or suggestion.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: From the report I would take it that nine employees were discharged for cause.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: And the others because of their connection with the union?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
The others because of their connection with the union. That is what I would take from reading the report. What I want to point out again is that despite the fact that these employees had the right to organize under the laws of Canada; despite the fact that a commissioner had found that they had that right and that there was no case against them; despite the fact that he recommended that they be put back in their positions. up to the present time only a very few of them have been permitted to go back to work.
I am sure the Minister of Labour will pardon me for quoting from a New Year's message he delivered at the end of 1936, published in the Labour Gazette of January, 1937. The minister expressed the right of association much better than I could when he said:
In connection with recent strikes in Canada there have been frequent complaints that certain employers have denied to their employees the

right of association and have summarily discharged men and women who have been active in the organization of labour unions. It is necessary to state in the clearest terms that the right of association is a civil right, long established by law and usage.
That established law did not help the employees of the Burns company who lost their jobs and are still out of employment. I continue:
It was affirmed with special reference to Canada by an order in council of July 11, 1918 (P.C. 1743). It was proclaimed explicitly in the treaty of Versailles at the close of the world war. To deny the right of workmen to combine in any lawful organization they desire for the promotion of their common welfare is an open invitation to extremists to preach the futility of collective bargaining as an alternative to direct action.
In other words, to deny the right of organization tends toward a breaking of the law in other directions. If that is true-and I maintain it is

then it is incumbent upon this house to see that what the law allows, the law shall guarantee. I quote:
The right of association for legitimate purposes should be respected in the national interest and labour should not be denied the means of organizing for collective bargaining. The right of employers to organize for all lawful purposes is not questioned in any quarter. Employers are not entitled in the same breath to protest against governmental regulation of industry and to deny to labour its right to resort to legitimate measures of self-help to voluntary association.
I submit that the Minister of Labour has stated our position very clearly in that paragraph. These days we hear a great deal about democracy. Very few liberal speakers-I do not use the word "liberal" in a party sense- speak on this subject without referring to the necessity of maintaining democracy. May I say that I am in full accord with that. I believe that people have come to recognize the value of democracy as they have never done before, even if it is not as complete as we would like it to be. But democracy is impossible without freedom of organization. We measure our political democracy by the extent to which various classes in society are represented in government, and to make our political democracy worth while we must have economic democracy. Our economic democracy will be measured by the extent to which the various factors in our economic life share in its direction. The workers cannot share in the direction of industry until such time as they are organized. The industrial union by means of which the worker has some share in arranging the terms upon which he gives his labour, either of hand or brain, is the first step to that fuller democracy to which I hope we are travelling.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
Whenever I think of democracy my mind goes back to a visit to the Scandinavian countries about a year and a half ago. I was impressed with the reality of democracy in those countries, and I am convinced that their democracy and to a large extent the stability of their social structure are dependent upon the organization of the various economic groups within the countries. In Sweden the employers are organized; labour is organized; the farmers have their organization and, what may be equally important, the consumers are organized. I believe we would solve many of the problems created in this country by monopolistic industry if in some way or another we could organize the consumers. As one writer has put it, "The Swedish road to democracy is through organization. The fundamental units of this organization are economic ; their political parties reflect these alignments." Sweden with a population of a little over 6,000,000 people has 650.000 trade unionists. Canada with a population of something over 11,000,000, with about 2,000,000 workers who could organize, has not more than 250,000 trade unionists.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Is the number of trade unionists in Sweden greater than the number in the old country?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
My information is that a greater proportion of the workers in Sweden are organized in trade unions than in any other country. I am not stating that definitely; it is simply the information I have at the moment. Mr. Justice McIntosh, the commissioner in the Burns dispute, stated that a possible cause of the dispute was the inexperience of the management in dealing with trade unions. May I say that the use of the instruments of democratic procedure does not differ from the use of any other instruments. We must learn to use them before we can use them efficiently. The old saying that practice makes perfect is just as true of trade union organization and negotiation as it is of anything else. When a union is well organized; when a union has had considerable experience in negotiating with employers, it is very seldom that there is a strike; it does happen the odd time, but not very often.
I should like to quote briefly from an article which appeared in Harper's Monthly Magazine, of November, 1936, by Mr. Hubert Herring. This deals w'ith trade union organization in Sweden. It seems so good to me that I think it worth while to read it to the house:
The Swedish labour union serves to make some six hundred and fifty thousand individuals, representing perhaps one-third of the population of Sweden, partners in democratic control. These members study, they debate, and they participate. Knowing that the local union is a unit in the national union movement which dominates the social democratic party and that the social democratic party is the dominant party in the national parliament makes for responsibility and realism. The fantastic loses its charm. The Doctor Townsends and the Huey Longs and the Father Coughlins have the ground cut out from under them. The Swedish worker has no prejudice against the promised land of plenty, but he knows that the way is beset with practical problems.
When you find a trade union organized and dealing with practical problems, and when the employees meet their employers and know the practical problems with which the employer has to deal, then you find people who are open to reason and, as I said before, it is not very often one finds strikes and disorders developing under those conditions.
I notice that in his message in 1937 the Minister of Labour expressed the same sentiments as he had expressed in 1936, pointing out that many of the strikes during the year which had just closed were caused by workers wishing to bargain collectively, and employers refusing to meet them. May I quote these few words from that message:
Once these relations-
That is collective bargaining.
-are established between employers and employees, they supply the best possible guarantee of industrial peace. They facilitate the discussion of particular disputes in a spirit of tolerance and forbearance. They also encourage a sense of obligation on the part of both to the community at large.
I agree with that, too. In effect he is saying that collective bargaining makes for good citizenship, and that it makes both employer and employee more socially minded. They recognize that a social interest is involved and that industry is not something which concerns only those actually engaged in it, but that it also concerns the community at large.
In the light of what I have said I would ask the government to give the most careful consideration to the bill before it decides that nothing can be done. If the bill is not acceptable because of its construction, we shall be only too happy to support any measure which would accomplish the end in view, namely to give the workers the right to associate in organizations of their own choice, in fact, as well as in law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of the law cited by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), or the soundness of his statement when he says that this bill is ultra vires because it intrudes on

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
provincial jurisdiction, yet I intend to vote for the bill, if it is only as a friendly gesture towards trying to do away with the principle of what is known as the black list on the Pacific coast.
It is true that last fall there was a bill passed in the provincial house, known as the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act, which was supposed to be a universal cure-all, but it appears to be more spectacular than useful from the working man's point of view. That the black list still exists is indicated by statements I have under my hand. Some trouble arose in a lumber camp, and submissions were made to the government. One comment is as follows:
One affidavit stated, among other things, the boss told me that as far as my work was concerned there was none better, but that it was impossible for him to rehire me. In giving his reason for not hiring me, he said, "there is no use of telling you there is no black list, because you know better."
A second affidavit states: "Upon asking if my work was satisfactory he said it was very satisfactory, and that he had nothing against my work whatsoever. He informed me that I would not be hired on account of my union activities in the camp in the previous year."
I also find that the employment office which sends lumber workers to the camps makes those workers sign a slip, one clause of which reads as follows:
It is understood I will not invite or allow any person in the camp or on the premises without the owner's consent.
The paper from which I quote, the B.C. Lumber Worker, goes on to say that that is rank intimidation. I do not know whether it is that or not, but certainly it is an interference with the liberty of the people. It would be just the same for a man to rent a house, and tell his tenant that he, the owner, would prescribe as to who would or would not be entertained in that house.
There is no doubt that, despite the provincial bill, the black list is still in existence. It is a very fruitful source of profound dissatisfaction on the part of many loggers. Therefore, if it is only a gesture along this line, I shall support the bill if it ever comes to a vote.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, I cannot do more than give a brief introduction of what I had hoped to say on this bill to-night. As it has been presented to the house, the bill has taken the form of an amendment to the criminal code. As such it was dealt with by my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when it was before the house some
TMr. Neill.]
little time ago. It was stated then by the Minister of Justice-and I repeat it now- that the right of workers to form or to join trade unions has the full support of this government.
Freedom of association has been proclaimed on several occasions by the dominion government.
It may be within the memory of some hon. members in the house to-night that during the great war, in order to meet rather grave conditions of industrial unrest, an order in council was passed which very clearly affirmed the right to organize. It took the form of an assertion of the existence of the right to organize, and there was no suggestion at the time that the dominion parliament had power to deal with the question in any way other than by declaration.
Mr. Speaker, it is nine o'clock.

speechtext: I believe we are on section 5 of the bill, the last section. The leader of the opposition called my attention to the fact that my previous suggestion, namely that on the title we might discuss general matters connected with the bill, would be of little avail, because there is no title. I therefore suggest it would be appropriate for hon. members, such as the hon. member for Marquette and other hon. members who wish to make observations on the general workings of the act, observations which would not come directly under any of the sections of the bill, to make those observations on section 5, which deals with the method of terminating the act in the various provinces.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: A very appropriate place.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, what I say will probably be misinterpreted, no matter how carefully I may choose my language; nevertheless, I shall take the risk, if risk there be. I therefore state I am not attacking or impugning the principle of the act. I realize there is no intention in the amendment before the committee to impugn the principle of the

Farmers' Creditors Act
act; it is simply to place the responsibility perhaps where it should belong, namely on the provinces, by proclamation.
What I wish to discuss is the question of deliberate default on the part of a debtor, and to suggest what I am sure every member of this house will agree on, that some remedy should be applied to deprive any person of the benefits of the act who is entitled to and does receive them and who thereafter wilfully evades the corresponding obligations and undertakings and defeats the very purpose of the act itself. What I say cannot be applied to an honest debtor, but certainly it may be applied to a dishonest debtor. In order that I may draw my conclusion I shall have to inform the house of a case which, I think, can hardly be duplicated in the dominion, and one which, I believe, justifies the remedy that I shall propose at the end of my remarks. Therefore I shall have to ask the house to bear with me if I am a little lengthy.
The case concerns a property in Manitoba which was sold under an agreement of sale in 1930. The price was 810.000, interest 6 per cent, and the payments were spread over a period of years. There was no cash payment. The purchaser entered into possession of the land but did not make any payments for some considerable time, and ultimately the estate, which was in the hands of executors, decided that they must take steps to protect their interests. In Manitoba the first thing to be done is to obtain a certificate from the provincial debt adjustment board. After sixteen months I was able, on behalf of the estate, to obtain that certificate. As soon as I obtained it, an appeal was taken by the purchaser of the farm to the county court judge. The appeal was heard and dismissed, and proceedings were therefore taken by way of foreclosure in the court of king's bench, Manitoba. When the action was before the court a dispute note was filed. It was purely a bogus dispute note. The whole intent of the agreement of sale, as they said, was that the proceeds of the farm would pay for the purchase price. When the matter was brought before Mr. Justice Adamson no representations were made by the defendant except for the purpose of obtaining time in which to redeem. I pointed out to the judge at the time that to give time for redemption would mean that this man would just wait until the period had almost elapsed, and then would apply under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Six months was given to redeem. This expired on March 16, 1935, and on that date the purchaser filed a proposal with the official receiver. The matter was
heard before the official receiver and no agreement was arrived at. An appeal was then taken to the board of review, and after a hearing the board of review formulated a proposal. That proposal was objected to strenuously on the part of the estate because it was felt it amounted to a confiscation of the estate under the sanction of law. We had a strong case; but apparently it was not strong enough, for the board of review still maintained their proposal, and ultimately it was filed in accordance with the act.
In order that the house may fully understand the position, the only payments which this man made under this S10.000 agreement amounted to 8616.42 over a period of seven years, or an average of S88 a year, and the estate, in order to protect the farm, had to pay taxes to keep it out of tax sale, and had to pay insurance to the amount of $370.98, and on October 31. 1937, there were taxes due amounting to $387.53. In other words, the money paid by this farmer from 1930 to 1937 was less than the amount paid by the estate, including taxes for which the estate is liable. He had had the farm about seven years, and all that the estate has received is the amount stated.
When the matter was before the board of review the position was that this man actually owed, including the purchase price of the land, $19,000, and against that he had assets of S540 for stock, and the most meagre line of equipment to carry on operations. I do not suppose the assets, including stock and equipment, would realize more than $1,500. Yet the board of review made the order, and in that order they stated that the purchase price shall be reduced.. First, they take upon themselves to reduce the purchase price. There was a total indebtedness of about $15,000 at the time of the foreclosure action. The board of review reduced that to $7,500, almost fifty per cent of a cut. At that time it was shown that the defendant had $19,000 of debts. All the unsecured creditors except those with lien notes were absolutely wiped out, and after that the farmer continued with his operations under the board of review order. That board of review order is a precious thing in its way. It provides for the payment of this $7,500, which was the amount arrived at by one of the officers of the soldier settlement board. The board in Manitoba take this position, that they would arrive at the value of the land themselves and give no indication to the parties interested of how that amount was arrived at, and in consequence there is nothing you can say about the matter.
Farmers' Creditors Act

The farmer continued with his operations. During 1935, 1936 and 1937 he was bound under the order to deliver one-third share of the crop, and under the orders of the board that one-third share of the crop was to take care of all the obligations which he had to pay for the purchase price of the land. In 1935 that one-third share of the crop amounted to $49.80; in 1936 it amounted to $247.48, and in 1937, last year, it amounted to $16.47.
Provision is made by the board's order that the money received from the crop shall first be applied to municipal taxes; at all events the Manitoba act provides that one-third share of the crop shall be applied first to taxes; the purchaser has the right to pay the taxes and to hand over the receipt to the vendors, and that fulfils his obligation. As a matter of fact, all the money which the estate has received in three years has been paid out on account of taxes, and yet at the present moment there is $387.53 still owing in taxes.
AVhen the year 1937 came we were astounded to learn that this gentleman had leased the farm to another man altogether. He had left the farm and gone to the town of Virden in Manitoba, and is now, I am told, selling stock for an oil company from Brandon. I verified the facts and found that there was a lease of the farm given for three years. You talk of privity of contract, but there certainly is no privity of contract between the vendors and the present lessee. He is on the farm. In the meantime the old lady to whom the estate belongs, a very dear and beautiful English lady of seventy-five, is living in a small cottage on an adjoining quarter section belonging to her son, and looking over the fence at her beautiful home occupied by a stranger who has no interest in it.
Naturally one felt annoyed at circumstances such as these, and I was endeavouring to do all I could; so I communicated then with the board of review, pointed out the circumstances, told them of the hardship, and they realized it, but they said they could do nothing. And why? Because they had already given their proposal; it was filed in the court, and therefore they were functus officio and could deal no further with the matter. I communicated with officials in Ottawa and got the same answer from them. In fact, the letter I received indicates two widely different points of view with regard to certain matters of which I shall speak shortly. At all events, after all the efforts in order to get some place where the estate could regain the farm, we came to the question whether what we should do would -be done

under the rules and regulations of the act. In these rules and regulations there are two clauses, 48 and 49, which I am going to read.
48.	The official receiver or any creditor may, after giving such notice to the debtor as the court may in the circumstances require, apply to the court for an order setting aside a proposal because the debtor has-
There are four reasons.
(a)	made a fraudulent or preferential conveyance, gift, delivery or transfer of any of his property;
(b)	with intent to defeat or delay his creditors, departed or remained out of Canada;
(c)	assigned, removed, secreted or disposed of any of his property with intent to defraud, defeat or delay his creditors;
(d)	conducted himself to the satisfaction of the official receiver in such manner as indicates bad faith towards his creditors.
49.	In the case of any application made under the next preceding paragraph, the court may order that the proposal be annulled, and such an order shall be deemed to be a final disposition of the proceedings.
Would it not be imagined, reading that, that these words mean exactly what they say, and that the official receiver or a creditor may, after giving such notice to the debtor, apply to the court for an order setting aside the proposal? But when I make the request of the official receiver of the district in which this land is situate, and ask him to make the application to the court, which in this case would be the county court, he, with instructions from the board of review in Winnipeg and also perhaps from the officers in Ottawa, takes the position that that refers only to a proposal which is either before the official receiver or the board of review. I cannot understand the reasoning of it and I cannot convince the other side that my reasoning is correct.
For instance, an application is made to the official receiver. The hearing is set; the witnesses appear, and then if necessary it goes on to the board of review. What in the world is the use of making an application to the court to prevent the issuance of an order when it is at that moment before the official receiver and before the board of review? If there are evidences that any of the four subsections which I have read have been contravened by the applicant, the farmer who is applying, all that need be done is to bring that matter before either the official receiver or the board of review and he will not get the order or the composition that he is seeking. That would seem self-evident, and I am informed it is the fact that there have been applications to the court in that particular district on that very ground. But why the necessity for it I do not know, because surely if a litigant comes before the

Farmers' Creditors Act
court with impure and unclean hands, those who are in the position of authority and to whom he must appeal would certainly not formulate any proposal but would simply refuse to do anything with it. If it only means that, that remedy is in the hands of the official receiver or the board of review; why should this be placed in the act at all? They say, of course, that lawyers always disagree, when they are paid for it. I submit that there are many differences of opinion in the courts with regard to the matter. It arose in one case in Manitoba, the Manitoba farm loan case, where one of the judges, Judge Richards came out and stated categorically that rules 48 and 49 did not apply to a proposal that had already been formulated by the board and had reference only to the proposal when it was before either the official receiver or the board of review. As against that, in the same judgment, Judge Prender-gast fakes the position that rules 48 and 49 are applicable. Judge Dennistoun made only a casual remark, and the other two judges made none. But it has happened that in other cases, in Alberta and also in Saskatchewan, there is a direct conflict of opinion among the judges as to whether rules 48 and 49 apply, and the consequence is that to-day the law is so muddled that no one knows where he is at. It happened in the course of my negotiations that it was suggested to me by a very high authority in Winnipeg-I do not mind saying that it was Mr. Justice Montague, judge of the board of review-when dealing with this matter, that he thought, his board of review being functus officio, their jurisdiction ended as soon as the proposal had been formulated, but we might invoke bankruptcy proceedings and thereby attain the object for which we were applying. The leader of the opposition referred to a case which I have read, the case of the Commercial Life Assurance company v. Strynadka, 1 Western Weekly Reports (1938), page 479. That decision states that where a debtor has defaulted in complying with the terms of the proposal confirmed by the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, chapter 53 (dominion), section 19	(2) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1927, chapter 11, cannot be invoked to support an application to the court to have the proposal annulled and the debtor adjudged a bankrupt. The advice I received from the head of the board of review in Winnipeg has been nullified-naturally must be-by the judgment of the appellate court in Alberta; and to-day we are in this state, that there are no judgments before the court as to how a creditor can arrive at a place where he can annul a proposal.
It may be suggested that I might take another action of foreclosure after default had taken place; but the unfortunate thing about that is this, that default has not taken place under the terms of the order of the board of review. The man has delivered the one-third share of the crop each year; in consequence he has lived up to that order and therefore we cannot invoke that procedure. We are apparently debarred from invoking rules 48 and 49 by reason of the dictum of the judge of the board of review in Winnipeg and also of the officers of the crown here. Where are we to go? I submit to the Minister of Finance that such a situation cannot be allowed to continue. The procedure in order to file a proposal and to have it formulated by the board of review is an informal proceeding, the cost of which is so little that there can be no objection to it. But I submit that no creditor should be obliged to make the law in courts when we here are dealing with the act, and we can remedy the act and make it so clear and unmistakable that there can be no doubt in the minds either of creditors or of the courts as to what exactly is intended. I submit that a creditor who is being defrauded by a debtor should surely have the same rights-inexpensive, informal, if you like-as are accorded to the defrauding debtor when he makes his proposal.

speechtext: My hon. friend is not alleging fraud in this case.

speechtext: I am alleging that the man is defaulting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: You say he delivered one-third of the crop as the order called for?

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes; but he has left the farm and gone off and is not a farmer now. The whole spirit of the act is defeated by the fact that the man is off the farm. He has left it to the lessee, and if that is not conducting himself in such a manner as to indicate bad faith towards his creditor I do not know what it is. I therefore suggest that rules 48 and 49 be amended and that it should be clearly stated that " the official receiver or any creditor may, after giving such notice to the debtor' as the court may in the circumstances require, apply to the court for an order setting aside a proposal," either before or after a proposal has been formulated by the board of review.
I make that suggestion to the Minister of Finance, and I ask him to take the matter up with the law officers of the crown and clarify the act so that the man who is endeavouring to defeat the principle of it shall be subject to the same remedies as he has invoked under the act, and that the act itself
Farmers' Creditors Act

shall supply that simple and inexpensive remedy to the honest creditor endeavouring to retain his property as against a debtor defaulting by his own act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: I shall be glad to have the suggestion examined. As I understand it, it would involve an amendment not to the act but to the rules. I shall have it looked into.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words applicable particularly to section 5 of the bill, which is the section that enables the governor in council by proclamation to provide that no proposal shall be filed in any province after a date fixed in such proclamation. I should like to add my remarks to those that have already been made urging the minister to cause the operation of this act to cease in the province of Ontario at as early a date as possible. I am unable to state, except from what I read in the newspapers and hear in this chamber, anything about the operation of the act in any of the other provinces; but I can state, from observation and first-hand knowledge of a good many of these cases, that whatever may have been the usefulness of the act when it was first passed, whatever necessity may have existed for its passage, it has entirely outlived its usefulness in this province.
The hon. member for Marquette gave a striking case in which a creditor in the west has been subjected to considerable hardship as a result of the operation of the act. I should like to put on record a somewhat similar case in which a creditor in Ontario has been defrauded-I do not think the term is too strong-and I do not adduce the details because they are of any particular interest in themselves; I cite them simply because the case is entirely typical of many such cases that have been dealt with by the board of review particularly in the course of the past three years or so. This is a case arising in the county of Essex in which the mortgage under consideration was made in April, 1923. It was a mortgage for 82,000, for ten years, at what was then the prevailing rate of interest, seven per cent, and the security was fifty acres of land, all of which was tillable. The repayments of principal were at the rate of 8100 a year. At the time the mortgage was made the mortgagor was a young farmer, twenty-four years of age, apparently quite capable of carrying on and making a go of his undertaking. He borrowed the 82,000 to retire a former mortgage, and the mortgage of which I am now speaking then became the first and only mortgage. The amount invested in the mortgage represented the savings of an elderly woman, savings that had been

accumulated as a result of very many years of hard work at low wages. From the date on which the mortgage was made in 1923 until 1926 the principal was reduced from 82,000 to $1,600, and the interest was paid promptly. After 1926 there were no further reductions in principal, but the interest was paid in full until the first of April, 1935. At that date the mortgagor owed nothing for taxes and he had some other debts, comparatively small. Having paid his interest up to the first of April, 1935, from which it might fairly be said that he had continued his interest payments throughout the worst of the depression, in the spring of 1935 he evidently learned of the act with which we are dealing, because from that date onward he ceased paying his interest and his other debts, and in the latter part of 1937 he applied under the act, his application coming on for hearing in January, 1938.
This is what was done. The two years of interest which he owed were wiped out; the mortgage was ordered renewed at the sum of $1,600 for a term of ten years from January 18, 1938 and the interest rate was reduced to three per cent. No repayments on account of principal were ordered until 1944, that is, five years in advance, and from 1944 on it was ordered that 875 on the principal should be paid annually. His unsecured debts were reduced by seventy-five per cent; it was ordered that the creditors must accept twenty-five per cent of their claims in full. As a result of that order great hardship was worked on this elderly lady who held the mortgage. Orders of that sort are becoming increasingly common.
My submission is that through the operation and administration of this act in recent years, *most of those whom it was designed to benefit; most of those who are worth keeping on the land and who are making an honest attempt to make a go of their farming operations, have been dealt with. They are either carrying on or else they have got off. And the present result of the continuance of the act is that many creditors Whose sole investment takes the form of farm mortgages have become impoverished; and on the other side of the picture, many men who should not be on the land at all, who are not making an honest endeavour to meet their obligations, are occupying farms which would be taken up by young, energetic and qualified farmers who cannot find a place. As a result of this situation the supply of mortgage money in Ontario has almost dried up, land values have been greatly reduced; young men who would otherwise go on the farm cannot get accommodation to buy stock, to make an

Farmers' Creditors Act
initial payment on a farm, to buy a few implements; and exactly the reverse situation to that which was intended to be created by the act has developed. I know of many such cases in London, because in that city, which is the centre of a very rich mixed farming and dairying community, there are many retired farmers who have come into the city with just enough money to see them through their declining years and who, as is common I think with most farmers in Ontario, have chosen mortgages for their investments. Many of them are in great destitution, some actually on relief, while a few miles out of London, occupying the premises on which they hold mortgages, are shiftless and, in many instances, dishonest farmers who have only sufficient energy and ability to convince the board of review that they have a right to stay on and a right to have their debts periodically pared down.
Therefore, in the interests of the very class for which this act was designed-the farmers -and in furtherance of the very object for which it was passed, namely, to keep as many farmers as possible on the farm, operating it and making a go of farming, I submit that in Ontario the act should be repealed at the earliest possible date.

speechtext: I have listened all afternoon to some hon. members complaining about the number of creditors who have been adversely affected by this act. When one remembers that more than 26,000 cases have been handled, it would imply more than human wisdom if there were not some cases in which there may have been unfair treatment. I personally could cite cases of people who invested their money, and now find that there has been a reduction which seems to them too drastic. But I would ask hon. members to remember first that this act deals with insolvency, with cases of bankruptcy in which the security against which the debts were placed has, in many instances, practically disappeared. When any concern goes into bankruptcy everyone connected with it has to take a loss. I am not suggesting that the creditors should take all the loss, nor yet should the debtor take all the loss. If the security has been reduced in value, the loss must be shared by both sides. And the figures speak for themselves. In the 26,365 cases that were dealt with under this act the average debt per farmer was $9,281.79. The total indebtedness-I shall just use round figures-was $158,000,000 registered against farms the value of which was only $112,000,000. In other words, the indebtedness was more than $46,000,000 in excess of the value of the farms.

speechtext:
The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has been assailed vigorously in many parts of Canada, but I want to assure the committee that so far as Saskatchewan is concerned the act has been beneficial. In fact, I think it is regarded as one of the most beneficial pieces of legislation we have on our statute books to-day. The reason for its introduction in 1934, and its nation-wide application, is just as apparent in Saskatchewan to-day-even more so 

than it was then. That condition need not be repeated, as it is well understood by members of the committee.
Parliament has recognized its responsibility in the matter of debt towards the people of Canada, and has taken certain steps to maintain a national equilibrium, and to enable business to continue. In the last revision of the Bank Act, for example, the rate was definitely fixed at seven per cent, with penalties attached for any infringements. That was made necessary because of the tendency- in fact, the practice-of the banks to>
charge whatever the traffic would bear-seven per cent, seven and a half per cent, eight per cent, eight and a half per cent and nine per cent. Western Canada, in particular Saskatchewan, was the victim of that practice.
Then, too, parliament has recognized its obligation towards debtors by its adjustment from time to time of arrangements with the soldier settler. Practically ever since the original arrangements were made, adjustments of one kind or another have been brought about. There has been a reduction in interest. Adjustments have been made in principal. Now we have before us a plan granting a dollar for dollar bonus to soldier settlers, which is to be offered them until 1941. With that plan I have no quarrel; I approve and endorse it.
Then, we have the Bankruptcy Act and its adjunct, the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act. The Companies' Creditors Arrange-51952-95J
ment Act, which was discussed here the other evening, provides a ready method for companies to adjust their indebtedness with their creditors, without the necessity of going through bankruptcy, retaining their good will, preserving something of their assets, and keeping the company away from the most destructive agency which we have, namely bankruptcy proceedings. I do not wish to enlarge upon the benefits of that act, but I say now that it has performed a very real service, and that it is a distinct advance in the administration of affairs between debtor and creditor.
Then, too, we have the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. The preamble to that measure asserts as its purpose enabling farmers to continue on the land and to support agriculture as the basic industry of the country. I am quite prepared to admit that it is predicated upon the bankruptcy of the individual farmer. So far as we are concerned, may I repeat that that act has been of beneficial effect, and has performed a very useful service. A good many have indicated to the committee the desirability of repealing the act, and have indicated some of the features in which it has worked a hardship. It has been stated that it is no longer serving a useful purpose. But the committee will observe from the recitation which I have just made, that no provision is made in any law to relieve the urban residents. There is nothing for the artisan. Is there any group of men who in the last six or seven years have suffered more than the artisans, the people identified with the building trade?
In Saskatchewan the situation is such that we have had only two loans under the Dominion Housing Act, notwithstanding the fact that last spring, during the months of Janu-* ary, February and March, certain loan companies advertised their willingness to take loans on that plan. But when applications were received, so many difficulties were placed in the way that it was not possible to effect a loan.
It may be said that legislation of this kind has been responsible for that situation. I am rather inclined to think, however, that it is the desire of those engaged in the money lending business to preserve western Canada, and Saskatchewan in particular, as a seven per cent, or better, loaning area, and not to permit any invasion by five per cent money.
Because of conditions, we were not able to take advantage of the home improvement plan. Under that excellent plan a smaller amount of money was loaned in Saskatchewan than in any other province of Canada, with the exception of Prince Edward Island. There-
Farmers' Creditors Act

fore it will be observed that there has been practically nothing in the province by way of work or wages for the benefit of the artisan.
Then, we must consider the clerk in the store, the office man and the commercial traveller. The commercial traveller has seen his living whittled away by degrees, has seen his commissions cut and his routes shortened, and has had to contend against competition of one kind or another-all of which meant a reduced income to the traveller.
Then we have the railway employees, thousands of whom have had to accept unemployment, or shorter hours and comparatively few working days per month. Those railway employees incurred obligations by building homes back in the days when agriculture was a thriving industry in western Canada, back in the days of 1927, 1928 and 1929. We must remember 1928, the year in which Saskatchewan alone produced 330,000,000 bushels of wheat, and when railway trains in the fall of the year were passing through Regina at the rate of one every twenty minutes, carrying complete train loads of grain to Fort William. It was during that period that these men incurred obligations by building their homes. Since that time they have passed through a period of intermittent employment, and find that the result of their efforts of bygone days is being gradually whittled away.
Then, too, we must remember the small business man in our towns, villages and cities, the man who finds that his business is being whittled away by the chain store, the great corporation, and that he is being gradually engulfed by their competition.
In addition to these, we have the civil servant who, like the railroad man, incurred similar obligations. In Saskatchewan the civil service has taken its share of the depression. Were the civil service of Saskatchewan put upon the same schedule of pay as the dominion service, it would cost that province nearly $2,500,000 more than it does at the present time. The civil service is a group of men and women who have borne their share of the depression.
Then we have the professional men, the lawyer, the doctor, the dentist, the veterinary surgeon, the surveyor, many of whom have been legislated out of business and who find their practices gone. That, Mr. Chairman, means that this very large group of responsible, honest and well-meaning citizens, desirous of fulfilling their obligations but finding themselves unable so to do, has been left to voluntary or provincial plans for debt adjustment. The provincial debt adjustment plan does what it can; but it is negative

rather than affirmative; all that can be accomplished there is to bring the parties together, and if no agreement is reached which the board considers fair, just and reasonable, the board may refuse the creditor the right to take foreclosure proceedings in the courts.
Our provincial government in conjunction with the dominion government made with the mortgage companies an arrangement applicable to the drought areas which provided for the wiping off of certain liens for seed grain, certain dominion liens, and also certain taxes, and the mortgage companies agreed to write off all the interest in arrears prior to January 1, 1935. They also agreed that there should be a six per cent rate of interest for ensuing years. But nothing was done with regard to the urban resident. I thought at the time it was intended that the six per cent rate of interest should apply to all mortgages, but such is not the fact. Mortgage companies are to-day in our larger centres collecting interest at the original rates under agreements which were made back in 1925, 1926, 1927, 192S and 1929 or thereabouts. That leaves that great group of men and women the one alternative of bankruptcy. And, Mr. Chairman, you will recall the scathing indictment of bankruptcy that was delivered the other evening by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). It is little wonder that the fear of the farming population with regard to bankruptcy proceedings is shared by the urban resident, and that they are resorted to only as a last resort. If anything were needed to complete the indictment of bankruptcy and bankruptcy proceedings in addition to what was said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George the other evening, it was supplied by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when, speaking on the second reading of this legislation on June 11, 1934, he said:
One of the difficulties that gave me the gravest concern about the legislation is the very circumstance to which attention has now been directed. There has grown up such resentment against some of the corporate trustees, on the part of those who have had to deal with them, that I say to the committee frankly I was amazed at the vigour of the protest that came to me from time to time, and during the last few months, in connection with matters of this kind. One of them has been discussed in a legislature, and one of them was discussed the other day in one of the courts of the country, and in the most vigorous terms the judge said that he intended to report the matter to the superintendent in bankruptcy. My experience has been, in connection with the farming population-that is in respect of voluntary assignment; and it does not apply to the province of Quebec at all-that they have complained, first, of expense, and secondly, that corporate trustees are without a soul, without any sympathetic attitude towards them at all.

Farmers' Creditors Act
Such is the indictment of bankruptcy proceedings from two very prominent men, and there are many others who could add their testimony to that which has been already cited. May I say that it is to the tender mercies of the Bankruptcy Act, which has been described in such eloquent terms, that we are leaving this very large group of urban residents.
It is true that some results are achieved from time to time by voluntary adjustment. It is also true in Saskatchewan, under our voluntary debt adjustment board, that some seven hundred foreclosures of urban property have been permitted. I should in fairness to the board say that in many of these cases, possibly all of them, there was an accumulation of principal, interest and taxes far beyond the present-day value of the property and that it was not possible to work out an adjustment.
Just a year ago there was presented to the Saskatchewan legislature a petition bearing some thirteen thousand names, and that petition is abundant evidence of the fact that there was in the urban centres of that province a real need for the application of the provisions of this act. There is need for the creation of tribunals where those who had in the good days incurred obligations might go and have them adjusted on a basis on which they could pay and which would give them a new hope for the future. On the basis of that petition the matter was debated in the Saskatchewan legislature and a resolution was passed containing a number of clauses, of which I should like to refer to numbers three and five. Clause three reads:
That the scope of the said act be widened to permit of home owners in cities, towns, villages and hamlets making proposals under the act to obtain adjustment of mortgages, agreements for sale, liens and other encumbrances on their homes.
And five:
That the provisions of the act be extended to make it applicable to retail merchants and traders so as to enable them to claim the benefit of the act.
You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that the resolution asks for the application of the provisions of this act to urban home owners and also to retail dealers, and in making that recommendation the legislature had in mind just the very fear which has agitated the mind of the urban resident with regard to bankruptcy proceedings and what he has come through during the last seven years.

I shall come to that in just a moment, if I may.
It may be asked why we should protect these people and to what extent the protection should apply. I hope that hon. members will not think I am narrow or parochial in my discussion of this matter; but as it is one of the principles of this bill that its jurisdiction be limited to provinces. I am dealing with my own province only. In that province there are seven cities, eighty towns and three hundred and eighty-five villages, with a population something over three hundred thousand. The function that those cities, towns and villages serve is a service to agriculture. It is true that their prosperity depends upon a prosperous agriculture, but likewise a prosperous agriculture depends upon the service which those towns, cities and villages give. They are complementary; they are interlocking; and just as any country depends for its future upon a prosperous agriculture, an agriculture that is carried on by farmers who own and have a substantial interest in the farms which they are cultivating, so, too, a prosperous town, city or village can only be and remain such where a substantial number of its residents own and occupy their own homes.
The results of the situation which I have outlined are these, that those people have experienced a period of drought and all the climatic disasters which have visited our province; they have also been victims of the depression; they have to maintain themselves to-day on a basis where the rentals are 25 -7 per cent higher than they were in 1913, where the cost of everything that enters into their households is lli per cent higher than it was in 1913; and these very people cannot collect the accounts that are owing to them by the agricultural population, by reason of conditions, by reason of legislation. Under this act and by voluntary adjustments they find that their own accounts have been substantially reduced. They find their ratio of profit in the carrying on of their business is greatly reduced or has gone altogether. They find that on
Farmers' Creditors Act

mortgages and on agreements for sale of which they are covenantors the interest has piled up; and may I say this to eastern Canada, that it is not at the rates of interest which are enjoyed and regarded as commonplace here.
A few minutes ago the hon. member for London said that there was no money available for loans on farms in Ontario. Within the last few days I have had several conversations with a gentleman in Ottawa who informed me that there is active competition to-day in this city for loans on city properties. He also volunteered the information that they had not known in the last fifteen years a loan exceeding 6 per cent interest, and that most of the loans during that period had been on a basis of 5 and 5J per cent. I have seen mortgages on western homes varying all the way from 7 per cent to as high as 22 per cent. It is no wonder that on such a basis interest has piled up. Likewise taxes have increased. Urban centres have a relief problem. Our own city pays 20 per cent of the entire cost of relief, pays all of the administrative expense, carries the medical bills for relief recipients, as well as dental bills, opticians' bills, hospital bills, and a hundred matters of that kind. In the last five years we have seen our assessment grow from forty mills to fifty-one mills; and I sometimes wonder when I hear our Toronto friends complain about an assessment of around thirty-two or thirty-three mills and complain very bitterly because there is a possibility of that assessment increasing during the next year on account of relief.
There is also a tendency, in fact a very marked effort on the part of mortgage companies to recoup as far as possible some percentage of their losses in agricultural loans by continuing the prevailing rates of interest and insisting upon the letter of the bargain from their urban mortgagors. Then, too, farmers have moved into the city, and I could give the committee a number of distressing cases of that type, where farmers have sold their land, taken the cash payment, bought a home in the city and assumed a mortgage on that home. They now find themselves without any revenue from their farms, and are unable to get any adjustment with or any protection from the mortgagees who have the mortgages on their homes. They are without revenue and are about to lose what interest they have in their own homes.
There is another reason for the situation that has arisen. Times without number during the years 1920 to 1930 mortgagees refused to accept prepayment of their mortgages. They

have also refused to accept payment of instalments in arrears unless accompanied by a bonus of three months' interest. If mortgagees had been willing during those years to accept prepayment of their mortgages there would not be nearly so much difficulty or trouble to-day, but they refused so to do, and are now lamenting the results of that refusal.
In addition to this increased overhead, these accumulations of interest and taxes, every one of these men and women in employment in our urban centres, irrespective of their location, has had to accept a substantially reduced income. It is not possible for these men and women on the basis of their present-day income to meet obligations that were incurred in 1928 and 1929. It therefore seems to me to be part of our obligation that we should seriously consider a workable plan for the relief of these people who have accomplished so much, put up with so much, and faced a difficult period so valiantly.
I know that one of the difficulties is to work out a plan whereby the provisions of this act would be applicable to urban centres. In that regard I am going to refer to the original debate on June IS, 1934, in which the leader of the opposition, discussing this bill, and in reply to a question by Mr. Han-bury, made the following statement:
Offhand one would say, considering the kind of cases that will have to be dealt with, that here the whole arrangement is predicated on the ability of the man to pay. There need be no plan at all. If the board concludes that the man will never pay they should not make an arrangement. This is predicated on the assumption that the man has indicated, by his past history or by his present surroundings and conditions, his ability to pay something. He makes a compromise accordingly. . . .
The right hon. gentleman said that there need not be any plan at all, and perusal of many of the adjustments that have already been made under this act will show that quite evidently there was no plan at all. Because of past experience with the productivity of the soil, the board arrives at a basis on which it thought the man could pay. As I say, the leader of the opposition said that there need not be any plan at all, and then we find a number of others for whom a plan has been formulated. Prior to that there was a crop failure for some four or five years. It seems to me, therefore, that we can very well adapt the principle of this act to the urban residents, and that can be done by drafting a new part in language similar to that contained in the original act, making it applicable to urban centres. The principle of the bill would be the same; the purpose would be

Farmers' Creditors Act
complementary to the original purpose of the act. I say, Mr. Chairman, that the responsibility stands out as a challenge to us as members of the House of Commons to take some action with regard to the situation in which 300.000 people find themselves, and which w7as emphasized in the petition executed by 13,000 of them. They are the victims of depression, the victims of drought. They find an accumulated liability which it is impossible to meet, and any attempt to meet that liability in full will result only in an impairment of their future, so that they will approach the next economic cycle with assets diminished to such an extent that for them life in the future will amount to nothing more than one continuous chain of depressions. I ask that the committee and the minister in particular give serious and careful consideration to the formulation of a plan which will give some relief to urban residents.
