speechtext:
I would feel remiss in my duty if I did not place on Hansard my objections in general to this bill. I listened to the very capable speech of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), and I noticed his reference to adjustments made by the soldier settlement board in connection with reductions in interest and so on. That is all right; but I would ask, Who reimbursed the government for any reduction in interest or in principal? Naturally, the government. I never could quite understand, when this act was first passed, why they singled out the farmer and said to him, "With your particular creditor we are going to allow you to make application to have your debt adjusted, your interest and principal if necessary, and the creditor alone must stand the loss." I realize that in 1934 the farmers were in a very serious condition. The prices of their crops and of their live stock were very low; they were compelled to accumulate debts, and probably at that time something had to be done to assist them. But it is my contention that if we desired to save the credit of the farmer, it should, as a government, have agreed to pay the loss that any single creditor would have to sustain on the principal sum. That has always been my contention. I might say further that if that had been the case, boards of review, especially in Ontario, would have made much more careful decisions and reports. They would not have been so free to say to the debtor, "We shall cut your principal in half regardless of the creditor's situation."
I cannot help it, but it is impossible for me to illustrate my contention without citing a certain case. On one application in Bruce county the debtor did appear before the
official receiver first and then before the board of review. The board of review decided first to cut the unsecured creditors fifty cents on the dollar and do away with all interest, and they also decided that the principal of the mortgage should be reduced. But what did the debtor do after receiving his order? His first desire was to retain his credit in the town in which he dealt. The next day after the order was issued he came into town and paid in full his debts in that one particular place. He had only one idea-he wished to retain his credit. And this is what this act is doing to-day in Ontario; it is destroying the credit of our farmers.
Another case I have in mind was one in the county of York where the board of review had decided that payment of principal and interest should be made on the thirty-first of December in each year. The first payment was due on December 31, 1937. This farmer decided that he would realize all he possibly could before December 31. So he had a sale of his farm stock and implements on December 30, and the creditors had no right of action until January 1. Of course in that case the creditors lost all.
That is	one reason	why I	say	that theproclamation of this act should be dealt with in the very near future. I quite realize that to do away with it immediately might cause confusion.	I can also	realize	the	plight ofthe people of Saskatchewan, and why they desire this	act; it is	because	of	the highrates of interest and the drought, and probably people in the cities as well as on the farms desire it. But in regard to the extension of this act to town and village residents. I would say that the statement made	by	the hon.
member for Regina is quite correct, that in our towns and cities in Ontario we can borrow money. Transactions and transfers are taking place. But if the act be extended, we shall certainly have greater confusion, loss of credit and loss of value in our homes and real estate.
I believe the minister has on file a resolution from the county council of the county of Bruce; I think I forwarded it to him last year. That county council consists of a reeve from each township and each municipality in the county. Those reeves in turn represent the residents of their townships. Having spoken of this last year, and placed on Hansard the cost of this act, the way it was administered and the doubt it has caused in the minds of men who might desire to lend money on farm properties, I believe that it would be in the best interests of the farmers to have this act declared in the near future not in force in Ontario. I believe this would
Farmers' Creditors Act

increase the values of our farms and would give our young men and women an opportunity to borrow money when they desire to start out in life. To-day they have not that opportunity, unless they go to the Canadian farm loan board, and the restrictions in the act under which that board operates are very harsh. I hope the minister will give this matter his serious consideration in the near future.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Apparently the popularity of this act depends upon where you live. As far as western Canada is concerned, I think sufficient evidence has been presented this afternoon definitely to impress on the committee that this legislation was necessary, at least at the time it was enacted. I think all the western provinces already had debt adjustment legislation, which, however, could not adjust anything; it really only stayed proceedings, and adjustments were made in which voluntary concessions were given on both sides. Then this legislation came along and provided the necessary machinery to complete settlements. It has served a useful purpose. As far as the act generally is concerned, I would not hazard a guess as to what percentage of cases have been actually dealt with by the board of review itself, but I think it furnished an incentive for a great many voluntary adjustments made by individuals without going to either the official receiver or the board of review. That is all to the good. In the part of the country from which I come a great many of the adjustments, as far as the farmer and his creditors were concerned, were made voluntarily through the official receiver. That is the cooperative concession which has been made on all sides.
A great deal has been said about the effect the act had on the farmer's credit. I honestly believe that the credit of the farmer is better to-day after he has gone through the board of review than it was before, for the simple reason that he did not have any credit or he would not have gone through the board. Therefore, I think it is correct to say that his credit has not been affected. It is true the act has created some hardships and dissatisfaction, and there have been some abuses. Some of our merchants have suffered unduly; some of them have been treated unfairly, or at least it would appear that way. At the same time I think it is only fair to ask what they would have got anyway had the farmer not gone through the board of review. In most cases there would have been nothing.
I understand that ordinary bunkruptcy, legislation, if it could have been made applicable

to farmers, would have achieved practically the same result as this legislation has. But when it was not applicable to the farmer, then something else was necessary, some cheap form of procedure for adjustment of these debts. Had the farmer been able to avail himself of ordinary bankruptcy legislation, these creditors who are making such a cry to-day about the manner in which they have been used would have been in exactly the same position as they are under this board of review. So in that respect I do not think they have suffered. I just wish to emphasize again that the legislation has assisted in bringing about many voluntary settlements which otherwise might not have taken place. And strange as it may seem, instead of requests coming from western Canada to have the operation of the act discontinued, we are actually receiving requests to have it extended to other classes of people, particularly those in towns and villages, and merchants to some extent.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it hardly seems nearly four years since I stood in my place across the chamber and introduced this bill in the house. It was predicated upon two considerations. The first was that it was desirable to keep the farmers on the land. That was part of the preamble of the act, that they should be retained in possession of their farms. The second was that inasmuch as under section 7 of the Bankruptcy Act a farmer could not take advantage of the provisions of that statute, we should without making him bankrupt give him all the benefits which would accrue if he were able to take advantage of that statute.
The delay in introducing that measure, from 1930, was owing to the fact that there was grave doubt on the part of lawyers as to our right to introduce it at all. It was felt by many that it was within the sole jurisdiction of provincial legislatures and not of this parliament. However, in the session of 193233 we introduced the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act, and on reference to the court it was held to be intra vires. There was pending in the courts a case known as Larue and the Royal Bank of Canada which went to the privy council, and it was held that legislation of a certain kind was intra vires. Therefore, we concluded that we had the jurisdiction to introduce this statute as a bill, which we did.
I have been very much impressed with the criticisms which have been urged against this measure. They have been urged by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Tomlinson) to-night. But I submit that there has been a complete misunderstanding of the basis of

Farmers' Creditors Act
this legislation. Once it is understood, I cannot think for a single minute that there would be any objection to it so far as principle is concerned. The hon. member for Macdonald has referred to that principle. It is hardly necessary at this time to refer to the fact that legislation dealing with bankruptcy is very old in the British Empire. The theory of bankruptcy goes back almost to prehistoric days, to the dawn of civilization. When men began to make arrangements and to have institutions, they began to realize that an honest man should have another chance and that if his assets were divided ratably among his creditors, he should be discharged from further liability and given another opportunity to start in life. That is the theory of bankruptcy legislation.
Bankruptcy measures have been on the statute books of Great Britain for many years. We had a Bankruptcy Act in this country in the early days, but it was not found to be satisfactory and was repealed. In 1919 we placed upon the statute books what is now known as the Bankruptcy Act. The theory of bankruptcy is that all the assets of the individual shall be liquidated and his creditors shall receive ratably among themselves the proceeds of the sale of the assets. Obviously we could not keep the farmer on the land and follow that principle, so we provided that instead of his being sold out when he could not pay his debts, instead of his assets being realized upon and divided ratably among his creditors, he should be permitted to work out his own salvation on some scheme or plan which would be effective, having regard to all the circumstances of each case.
The hon. member for Macdonald pointed out quite properly a moment ago that voluntary arrangements have been made in a great many eases. Just as soon as it was apparent that this legislation was on the statute books, these voluntary arrangements became the order of the day. As soon as it was apparent that by voluntary effort and cooperation these arrangements could be carried out, when the extent to which the statute went was not generally known, these settlements were made; but when it became apparent that the statute was of much wider consequence, then appeals to the boards of review became more numerous. It is for this very reason that the board of review is presided over by a judge. This is in order that judicial procedure shall mark the operation and conduct of the proceedings under the act. In other words, the true bankruptcy significance of the act should be apparent in the acts of the judge who presides over the board of review.
In many cases it was quite clear-this was particularly so in one province-that the official receivers went around soliciting business. That was done when they were paid on the basis of so much for each case. I looked at a return supplied by the Minister of Finance for all provinces, and I saw one community with less than 90,000 people where the activities of the official receivers were marked indeed. I am sure that if hon. members have looked at this return they will be struck with, shall I say the versatility of the official receivers and their great ability in getting business.
But what happened in other cases? First of all, we have the official receivers; then we have our board of review consisting of a judge and representatives of the creditors and the debtor. I wish I had the time to refer to the circumstances under which those provisions became part of the law of the country. However, I will say to the hon. member for Bruce that representatives of the loan and lending companies of this dominion came together here at Ottawa. I met them personally and spent the major part of half a day with them in the first instance, and later on a lesser time. They realized the situation was such that while it was not desirable that the farmer should come under the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, some proceeding in the nature of bankruptcy should be resorted to if we were to keep the farmer on the land and give him an opportunity to work out his own salvation.
Now, having gone that far, having had the official receiver and having had the board of review, we found that this question at once arose:	Can you deal with the secured
creditors? Here is a situation where you have a mortgage, where you have a bank with security, sometimes in the form of a chattel mortgage-could we deal with the secured creditor? Under a voluntary arrangement, except by consent, the secured creditors were not made subject to the provisions of the act; but just as soon as they went to the board of review where steps w'ere taken by the board to formulate a scheme, jurisdiction was conferred to deal with secured creditors. The result was and is that in many instances the secured creditors have had their security cut in half. There have been instances in which it has gone that far. Why? Because the value of the assets on which the mortgage was given was less than half the amount of the mortgage. In other words, the present value and the possible improvements that might take place determine the action of the board of review. In other
Farmers' Creditors Act

words, the board's action was based upon the present value plus probable improvement in value.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: That is where the matter of opinion enters which gives so much difficulty.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
With respect to the
first factor, there has always been a little difficulty; with respect to the second factor, there has always been much difficulty, for the simple and obvious reason that it was always most difficult for men to arrive at unanimity as to what the probable future would be. For instance, I have known cases in which opinions were expressed that the future would be rosy and bright, but unfortunately there was no rain the next year and the future became darker than the past. That position has arisen frequently in western Canada.
I put this question to the hon. member for Bruce:	Why should a farmer be denied
the benefits of the principle of the bankruptcy law? Bankruptcy law is one of the oldest marks of civilization. I said a moment ago that it is predicated upon the thought that an honest man who was willing to hand over all his assets to be divided among his creditors should be entitled to be discharged to start again free from judgment or action against him. Owing to economic conditions, the assets of the farmer had changed in value so that it was quite impossible to realize upon them anything like the amount of his indebtedness. He is now receiving the same measure of justice as though he were a trader; but instead of selling out his assets, he is retained in possession of them and he works out over a period of years his economic salvation. That is the purpose of the act. Why should we say that he is not entitled to it as much as the trader? Why should we say that we have a bankruptcy law passed in this country in 1919 for the benefit of all those who seek to avail themselves of it, and not make it available to the farmer?
But the farmer of course, did not wish to go through bankruptcy in the way in which that term is technically and legally used. So we provided that instead of his making an assignment under those circumstances, instead of his having an assignee in bankruptcy, or a trustee in bankruptcy, we provided this simple machinery at the cost of the state to enable the farmer who creates new wealth-the greatest creator of new wealth outside of those who discover gold and petroleum, the greatest continuous producer of new wealth-to have his assets-including mortgages, and including his secured creditors-ratably divided among them, not on the realization of his
[Mr. Bennett.1
assets, but on the estimate of their present value, together with an opinion-which is an estimate-of what the future would bring to that man. That was the theory.

When I heard the hon. member for Wey-burn to-night talking about 8158,000,000, I thought one must realize how vast a sum that is. Yes, over $50,000,000.
Now, this was not an arbitrary act. I have said that it is done by this board, in the ultimate analysis, and each case is dealt with on its merits. Would it be possible to have 26,000 cases dealt with, Mr. Chairman, by any group of men, without cases arising where there would be bitter criticism as to something with which they had dealt? I admit this, that when men deal with these things continuously they develop a bent to their minds either favourably disposed or otherwise to the creditor or debtor class. In this instance throughout Canada I think it is fair to say that the sympathy of the board is given to the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

subtopic: BOARDS OP REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILINO PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think there is no doubt about it. And in the light of that sympathy, it may have created in the minds of some of us the idea that the law has not been strictly enforced; for the basis of the legislation, as I said in the house four years ago, and again to-night, was insolvency. Let there be no misunderstanding about that, because we could not be here at all if it were not for the fact that the basis of it is insolvency.
Look at the statute. The statute itself makes it perfectly clear in section 6, that it must be that. It states:
(1)	A farmer who is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due may make a proposal for a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement either before or after an assignment has been made.
(2)	Such proposal shall be filed with the official receiver who shall forthwith convene a meeting of the creditors and perform the duties and functions required by the bankruptcy act to be performed by a trustee in the case of a proposal for a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement.
And the chief justice of Canada, when this statute was before the court, summarized it as follows:
The provisions of the statute are made a part of the general system for the administration of the assets of bankrupts and insolvents established by the Bankruptcy Act, and they come into operation only where a farmer who is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due makes a proposal for a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement.
That is the language of the Supreme Court of Canada. Bearing in mind that that is the
basis of all these proposals, the basis of this legislation, can one for a single moment say that, as was said by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, these men were not insolvent? If they were not insolvent the board had no jurisdiction, and the courts of the country could issue a prohibition against them proceeding. But when you hear an hon. member of this house or elsewhere say that men were not insolvent, I say: Who has failed in the discharge of his duty? The board had no right to hear such cases. If they did so, that is not because the law is bad, but because it is administered badly. It is because those who had no right to hear have heard. But I am bound to say my examination led me to the conclusion that I have not yet been able to find a single case where an allegation was made that the man was not insolvent that the evidence did not disclose that he was hopelessly insolvent. How could he be otherwise? He files there a statement of his debts, and you see at once what they are.

There are some further . matters I desire to deal with, I am sorry to say, but-

I think it should be made abundantly clear that the statute is within itself a charter which controls and governs the whole administration, and that it should not be a question of any application being made under a bankruptcy act, which, of course, if applied, does not apply in the case that arose in Alberta, for the reasons given by the chief justice. I think we should deal with that.

Then, we should deal more broadly than has been done, with the question of who is a farmer, because we followed largely the definition in the Bankruptcy Act when we were dealing with that. We should deal with the case in which farmers are incorporated. For instance, many families have incorporated themselves as limited companies, those families living on the land. We should not deny them the benefit of this because they have studied the problem and have taken this form of conducting their business.
There are two or three other cases to which I should like to make reference, but it is now eleven o'clock.
